strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: dependence of LLM judgments on the evaluator model. Decomposing evaluation into explicit checklist decisions provides a practical, inspectable scoring procedure without additional model training.

The experimental coverage is substantial: 12 evaluators across model families and sizes, with summarization and dialogue benchmarks plus QAGS. Reported correlation improvements are particularly substantial for some weaker evaluators; Llama3.1-8B improves from approximately 0.24 to 0.41 on SummEval and 0.11 to 0.46 on Topical-Chat.

Human checklist validation, component ablations, question-weighting experiments, binarized-baseline comparisons, and an inference-budget experiment provide useful evidence beyond headline correlations.

The pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript supplies seed questions, prompt templates, open-model identifiers, inference settings, hardware information, costs, and a code link. These provide a useful foundation for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central agreement results require verification. Table 25 reports G-Eval large-model groundedness α=0.0030 and κ=0.7288, although Table 12 identifies this output as binary. For the same complete binary annotation matrix, standard Krippendorff’s α and Fleiss’ κ should be nearly identical. Large discrepancies also persist after binarization in Tables 13–14. The paper needs to specify the annotation unit, α distance function, and missing-output handling, and audit the implementation. It is also unclear whether CheckEval agreement concerns individual checklist answers or aggregated text scores; these measure different quantities. This unresolved issue directly affects the headline reliability claim.

Several reported results are internally inconsistent. For example, Table 1 gives SEEval/Gemma2-9B a SummEval Spearman correlation of 0.49, whereas Table 22 reports 0.4269. Table 15 reverses G-Eval’s Topical-Chat Spearman and Pearson means relative to Table 24. These discrepancies warrant regenerating the tables from shared evaluation outputs. Main comparisons also lack uncertainty estimates despite claims of significant improvements; some strong-model gains are only 0.01–0.03. Paired confidence intervals should account for shared source documents or conversations.

The checklists do not always convincingly operationalize the intended dimensions. Table 27’s groundedness seeds emphasize conversational relevance, flow, and consistency without explicitly checking support from the supplied fact. Table 26’s relevance seeds reward retaining source terminology, potentially penalizing valid paraphrases. Human judgments that questions are acceptable do not fully establish construct coverage or correctness of the resulting evaluations.

The ablations only partially establish why the method works. Post-hoc binarization of holistic ratings does not isolate binary prompting from finer criteria and aggregation over multiple judgments. A comparison using the same decomposed criteria with Likert scoring would be more informative. The inference-budget experiment covers only one model and dataset, without demonstrating matched token expenditure. Additionally, variance across model-level correlations in Section 7.1 does not establish reduced variance of individual evaluation scores.

The human evidence supports a narrower conclusion than the discussion suggests. Correlations use only 20 summaries stratified by existing quality scores, while agreement covers only relevance. The six-rater κ=0.49 pools humans and LLMs and therefore does not specifically estimate agreement between those groups. There is no matched human Likert condition establishing improved human reliability. The reported 10,000 relevance decisions per annotator also conflicts with 100 summaries and the 26-question relevance checklist, which imply 2,600 decisions.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified in the manuscript, including complete substitutions for the augmentation prompts’ conditions and constraints, dated GPT model identifiers, and identification of the frozen augmented checklists used for each experiment. Overall, the useful approach and extensive experiments merit revision, but the unresolved agreement measurement and reporting issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present. An audited analysis and corrected documentation could reasonably be prepared for the next cycle.
